articles.title: Uncertain local governments
articles.content: THE battle between the Election Commission of Pakistan and the provincial and federal governments has been an almost permanent feature of Pakistan’s electoral scene since 2010, when the responsibility for holding local government elections was entrusted to the Commission under the 18th Amendment. Currently, the ECP is fighting a four-way battle — with the provincial governments of Punjab and KP, the federal government, and the cantonment boards — for LG elections in the two provinces, Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT), and the cantonment boards. The LGs in Sindh and Balochistan (except in the largest district of Quetta, where the entire term passed without election) have yet to complete their terms. The ICT LG election is the most disappointing case. The last LG election in ICT was held in November 2015. Its five-year term ended on Feb 14, 2021. Under the Elections Act, 2017, the new election was to take place within 120 days after the previous LGs’ term ended, making June 15, 2021, the due date for the next election. For more than five years, the ECP and the federal government have been haggling over legal points and the possible date of the next election. Since 2021, the ECP has issued the election schedule four times and carried out fresh delimitation five times. Each time it has had to eat humble pie by withdrawing the schedule as the federal government changed the goalposts and amended the LG election law. The latest in the series was the ICT Local Government (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, promulgated on Jan 10, 2026, which drastically changed the capital’s LG system. However, the ordinance lapsed in September 2026. While parliament is going through the motions of converting the lapsed ordinance into an act of parliament, the ECP maintains that the old ICTLGA, 2015, stands resurrected after the ordinance lapsed and, therefore, issued apolling scheduleon Oct 25, fixing Dec 20 as polling day. Looking back at the federal government’s track record, the new act is likely to pass in the next few days, after which the ECP would have no choice but to withdraw the schedule and begin preparations anew. The case of KP is not very different; the terms of the LGs expired on June 19, 2026, after which new elections should have taken place by Oct 20, but the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Local Government (Amendment) Act, 2026,was passedand became effective on July 16 this year. It changed the size of the village and neighbourhood councils. The ECP strongly objected to the amendment, termed it a delaying tactic, and asked the provincial government to review the law. In the meantime, the ECP is proceeding with preparations to hold the LG polls, except in 12 districts where the law and order situation doesn’t permit polls. The ECP has yet to issue an election schedule. Still, it remains to be seen whether the National Assembly, which has the legislative powers of the KP Assembly after the proclamation of emergency, will amend the LG law or whether the elections will be postponed yet again on some pretext or the other. The ECP is battling both the federal and provincial governments that are reluctant to hold LG polls. All formalities for holding the LG election in Punjab have beencompletedby the ECP and the Punjab government under the Punjab Local Government Act, 2025. If finally held, this will be the first LG election in roughly 11 years. The election was supposed to be held in May 2022, but a series of new laws and amendments kept postponing it. Although the Punjab government ministerial committee and the ECP agreed to hold the election in three phases between Dec 15 and Jan 15, the Punjab government changed its mind and asked the ECP to defer the election until April 2027 because of dense fog and school exams in December. The ECP immediately rejected the new dates and asked its secretariat to prepare an election schedule based on the earlier agreed dates. The election schedule has not yet been issued; one should wait to see which side blinks first. The election to 43 cantonment boards in the country was due on Aug 8 as the four-year term of the previously elected boards expired on April 11, 2026. The cantonment boards’ election has an additional prerequisite: the ECP should receive the federal government’s request before holding the election. Reportedly, no such request has been received, and the ECP, given the legal requirement to hold elections within 120 days of the expiry of the term, is trying to reach out to the federal government. Regardless of the outcome of these efforts, the election to the cantonment boards is also overdue. These four stories lead to a single conclusion: both the federal and provincial governments are reluctant to hold LG elections on one pretext or another. The key flaw in the system is that while the ECP is responsible for holding LG elections, the governments and their legislatures alone write the LG laws. There is no bar on legislatures amending LG laws. As demonstrated repeatedly, the law can be amended after the announcement of the election schedule and even a few days before polling day, undoing all the preparation made by the ECP such as delimiting LG boundaries. The solution is for parliament to amend the Elections Act, 2017, and bar any amendment to the LG laws after the expiry of the LG term, so the ECP can prepare unimpeded and hold timely elections. As if these difficulties were not enough to make the future of LGs uncertain, another layer of unpredictability has been added by the possibility of carving out new provinces and, in the case of ICT, by the announcement that Islamabad may soon have provincial status. This may give the government yet another pretext to slow-walk LG elections. The writer is the president of Pakistan-based think tankPildat.president@pildat.org
articles.author: Ahmed Bilal Mehboob

articles.title: India’s water blackmail
articles.content: SINCE April 2025, when Indiaunilaterally suspendedthe Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), most scholarship has treated it as a political decision by the BJP-led NDA government. While it is true that the BJP has been developing a narrative that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi was ‘rectifying’ the ‘mistakes’ of the Nehruvian era, the decisions and developments during the past 18 months suggest that New Delhi is developing a long-term strategy to strangle Pakistan economically. India’s primary target in this strategic campaign is the Chenab river, which it is systematically converting into a long-term instrument of leverage to dictate Pakistan’s foreign policy, weaken its stance on Kashmir, and dominate bilateral relations. In the 18 months since it decided to keep the IWT in abeyance, India has aggressively leveraged this treaty vacuum to build a massive network of storage, regulation, and diversion infrastructure on the Chenab. New and accelerated hydroelectric power projects, primarily concentrated in the Chenab basin, have ballooned from a baseline capacity of 3,263 MW to 7,620.5 MW, supported by a massive financial outlay of approximately Indian rupees 414.04 billion. No single dam or diversion canal can permanently dry up a river. However, a highly synchronised, connected network of mega structures, coupled with diversion canals, can fundamentally determine who controls the timing and volume of river flow. India is trying to apply a two-pronged strategy, ie, increase storage capacity and enhance the ability to divert the Chenab’s water. India’s strategic roadmap involves five megaprojects alongside extensive local diversions. This includes Sawalkot (1,856 MW), Kirthai I & II (1,320 MW), Pakal Dul (1,000 MW), Ratle (850 MW), and Bursar Storage (800 MW). India’s infrastructure push began in May 2025, with the announcement of the tender for the Uri-II project (240 MW), followed quickly in June 2025 by the tender announcement for the Dulhasti-II project (260 MW). Activity accelerated in July 2025 with two major announcements — first, a tender for the removal of deposited sediments from the Salal Dam Reservoir, and second, the Sawalkot project (1,856 MW) tender under international competitive bidding. In March 2026, civil contracts were officially awarded for both the Uri-I stage II and Dulhasti stage-II projects, alongside the official tender announcement for the highly controversial Chenab-Beas Link Tunnel Project (Link-3). These aforementioned projects command a combined potential diversion and storage capacity of roughly 7.287 MAF. For years, New Delhi has strategically used international platforms and institutional levers to weaken Pakistan’s economic foundations. The Chenab-Beas Link Project is particularly consequential. With a reported budget of Indian rupees 23.52bn, it proposes to transfer water from the Chandra river, a major Chenab tributary, through an 8.7-kilometre tunnel into the Beas basin and onward through a 113km canal network to eastern Indian states. The proposed diversion of 1.9 MAF annually from the Chenab basin raises serious questions about compliance with Article III of the IWT. The threat of manipulation, or the Chenab’s vulnerabilities, poses a direct risk to Pakistan’s economic survival, social stability, and national security. The Chenab directly irrigates agricultural lands across more than 11 districts of central Punjab, the country’s undisputed food basket. These districts form the densest core of the famous rice-wheat cropping zone. This 11-district area accounts for about 22 to 25 per cent of Pakistan’s national food grain output. If India controls water flows during October to December or May to July, it may affect seasonal yields in this zone. In such a scenario, it could cause a direct blow of $9bn to $11bn to Pakistan’s economy. The broader impact would ripple through the national economy in several ways. Pakistan would be forced to spend billions of scarce foreign exchange reserves to import basic food commodities. Instead of generating $3.3bn to $4bn from booming rice exports, the country would face a multibillion-dollar trade deficit just trying to secure alternative grain imports. Second, any sustained restriction on, or unpredictable disruption to, these water flows would threaten the livelihoods of millions of farming households, while endangering crops and compromising national food security. Therefore, Islamabad must view India’s decision to place the IWT in abeyance as another dimension of New Delhi’s long-standing and coordinated policy of economic strangulation of Pakistan. For years, New Delhi has strategically used international platforms and institutional levers to weaken Pakistan’s economic foundations. New Delhi has been consistently trying to restrict Islamabad’s access to global capital and limit its trade capacity. A primary example is India’s aggressive lobbying within the Financial Action Task Force, where it has consistently tried to politicise technical compliance and block Pakistan’s removal from the grey list to discourage foreign direct investment and cripple its banking sector. Beyond regulatory warfare, India has systematically disrupted regional trade platforms, such as Saarc, effectively stalling economic integration across South Asia to keep Pakistan regionally isolated. Faced with this asymmetric threat, Islamabad’s response has been largely concentrated on the external front. Pakistan’s state apparatus has consistently pursued international legal and diplomatic channels. However, a dangerous policy gap exists on the domestic front. Ground-level preparedness is profoundly lacking. The agrarian communities, provincial irrigation departments, and economic sectors that will bear the immediate impact of India’s upstream infrastructure remain highly vulnerable. Pakistan lacks the modern water-storage infrastructure, optimised canal lining, crop-switching strategies, and real-time early warning systems needed to survive sudden changes in river flows. Hence, Islamabad should complement its legal and diplomatic efforts with urgent domestic reforms. Pakistan must declare a national water emergency, educate vulnerable communities in 11 districts of central Punjab that depend on the Chenab, expedite dam construction, and modernise irrigation. Without urgent preparedness, Islamabad will risk surrendering its agricultural security to Delhi’s water blackmail. The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.
articles.author: Khurram Abbas

articles.title: ‘L’état, c’est moi’
articles.content: THE insertion of Article 172(3) in Pakistan’s Constitution via the 18th Amendment was stupendously transformative, as it restructured the sovereign ownership of oil and gas. In the new constitutional scheme, the federation and the provinces were to be co-owners of oil and gas produced within the provinces. Yet, even after 16 years, the full benefits of this constitutionally bestowed co-ownership remain a covenant to be realised for the provinces. Around the time John D. Rockefeller was tapping into the Pennsylvania oil fields, India enacted its first oil legislation, the Petroleum Act, 1881. The legislation did not address ownership; rather, it regulated only the import, transportation, and possession of oil. The concept of private ownership of oil and gas resources, prevalent in the US and recognised by its supreme court as early as ‘Brown vs Spilman’ (1895), would never see the light of day in the Indian subcontinent; instead, de facto sovereign control would reign. The Indian Councils Acts, 1892 and 1909, and the Government of India Acts, 1915 and 1919,allowed the ‘central government’ to regulate oil, though they were gleefully silent on ownership. The Petroleum Act, 1934,did not rework this much. In any event, before the Government of India Act, 1935, the government of India was unitary and only thereafter became federal, listing ‘oil’ as a federal subject. This position persisted under Pakistan’s constitutions of 1956, 1962, and 1973, with ‘gas’ additionally listed as a federal subject. The 18th Amendment altered this legal paradigm by introducing Article 172(3), which proclaims: “Subject to the existing commitments and obligations, mineral oil, and natural gas within the province or the territorial waters adjacent thereto shall vest jointly and equally in that province and the federal government.” Cooperative federalism in the matter of oil and gas is being undermined. Though by virtue of Article 97 and 137 of the Constitution, the federal government retains executive authority over the regulation of oil and gas, the doctrine of ‘joint ownership’, together with oil and gas appearing in the Federal Legislative List, Part-II, means that the Council of Common Interests (CCI), by virtue of Article 154 of the Constitution, is empowered to formulate and regulate policies in respect thereof, and exercise supervision and control over related institutions. Clause 1.3.6 of the Petroleum Policy, 2012, enacted by the CCI, establishes a “reorganised Directorate General of Petroleum Concessions (DGPC) comprising federal and provincial representatives”. The de jure responsibility of the reorganised DGPC, inter alia, is to “decide the matters of grants, regulation, annulment and monitoring of all petroleum concessions” in the country, consistent with the Petroleum Rules, 2013. Regrettably, the provincial directors who are part of the reorganised DGPC have been given no de facto say in matters of “grants, regulations and annulments” of petroleum rights. The federal director at the reorganised DGPC deals with such matters unilaterally, recognising no situation where he can legally be outvoted, even by the four provincial directors combined. This approach is akin to Louis XIV of France declaring before the Parliament of Paris in 1655: “l’état, c’est moi” (“the state — it’s me”). The federal director, being a state functionary and one member out of a total of five who form the reorganised DGPC, cannot single-handedly claim to be the reorganised DGPC (though he does so and this ingression is less a personal trait, and more a projection of the federal government’s resolve to maintain its hegemony over oil and gas resources, even when the Constitution says otherwise). In ‘Wattan Party vs Federation of Pakistan’ (2006), the Supreme Court held CCI policies enacted under Article 154 to be binding on the federal government. Thus, if the latter takes exception to the implementation of a particular provision of the Petroleum Policy, 2012, vis-à-vis the role of the reorganised DGPC, then its remedy lies in referring the matter to a joint sitting of parliament in accordance with Article 154(7), and not in flouting the same. “The earth, and all that is therein, is given to men, for the support and comfort of their being. Yet being given for the use of men, there must of necessity be a means to appropriate them some way,” wrote John Locke in his Second Treatise of Government. The Constitution of Pakistan prescribes appropriation, which attends to the ownership, regulation, and control of oil and gas resources in a spirit of cooperative federalism. Yet the federal government’s functionaries can scarcely resist bellowing to their provincial counterparts, ‘l’etat, c’est moi’.
articles.author: Asad-ul-Mulk

articles.title: Off the back seat
articles.content: SOME time in the mid-2000s, I attended a conference for journalists in Goa. I remember very little of the panels. What I remember is going into town. Women everywhere, on scooters. Young women in jeans. Middle-aged women in saris, the pallu tucked in, a shopping bag on the footboard. Older women with grey buns and sensible sandals, weaving through traffic as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world. Because it was. This was next door. Same subcontinent, same heat, same chaotic roads, same aunties. So why was it unthinkable at home? In Karachi, a woman on a motorbike belonged on the back seat, perched sideways, dupatta wrapped tight so it would not catch in the wheel, one hand gripping the seat and the other holding a child. She was a passenger, in every sense. I never expected to see that change in my lifetime. Last month, a Gallup & Gilani survey found that 83 per cent of Pakistanis believe more women ride two-wheelers today than three years ago. In cities, the figure rises to 91pc. That is perception, not a headcount. But perception matters. People are noticing because there is something to notice. When the Sindh government launched its Pink Scooty scheme last year, offering free electric scooters to female students and working women, it hit an awkward problem. Only 154 women across the entire province reportedly held motorcycle driving licences in June. You cannot hand a scooter to a woman who is not legally allowed to ride it. So the scheme required a licence and offered free training to get one. Minister Sharjeel Memon told local media that over 50,000 women had applied for licences. From 154 to 50,000. Even allowing for a politician’s optimism, that is not a trend. That is a door swinging open. Consider the choices before a young woman with a job offer across town. It did not happen overnight. Karachi’s Women on Wheels programme, launched in 2019, recorded more than 3,000 registrations and trained hundreds of women to ride on the University of Karachi campus. The groundwork was laid quietly, by women willing to wobble, fall, and get back on. Why does this matter so much? Because in Pakistan, the road to a job runs through the question of how a woman gets there. Pakistan has one of the lowest rates of female labour force participation in the world. The World Economic Forum puts it at about 28pc. In our cities, World Bank research suggests it has hovered around 10pc for two decades. There are many reasons. Social norms. Childcare. Workplace harassment. But again and again, studies return to the same plain obstacle: transport. Consider the choices before a young woman in Karachi with a job offer across town. A rickshaw eats into her salary every single day. Ride-hailing costs even more. The bus is crowded, unpredictable, and, too often, a gauntlet of stares and hands. If no brother, father, or husband is free to drive her, the job may simply not be worth taking. A whole career can be lost to the problem of the commute. A scooter changes that arithmetic. It is cheap to run, cheaper still when it is electric. It goes where buses do not. It leaves when she is ready, not when someone else is. It turns a job across town from a family negotiation into a decision she can make herself. That is what economic independence looks like on the ground. Not a slogan, but a set of keys. And independence is the point. For most women, freedom is not an abstraction. It is the ability to earn, spend, leave, and return on their own terms. Financial freedom is freedom. A woman who can get herself to work can pay her own fees, support her parents, save for her children, and, if she must, walk away from a home that is hurting her. None of this is finished. Being seen is not the same as being accepted. Women riders still face harassment and disapproval. The change is clearer among urban, middle-class women than in villages. And reminders of how far we still have to go. In June, the minister told the Sindh Assembly that traffic police had been instructed to stop men riding the pink scooters after complaints that some women’s brothers had taken them over. I laughed when I read that. Then I stopped laughing. It says everything about who has usually held the keys in our homes. But the keys are changing hands. Slowly, unevenly, one licence at a time. The other day, at a traffic signal, a young woman pulled up beside me on a scooter. Nobody stared. I did, for a moment. Then I smiled. When the light turned green, she was gone. It looked like Goa. It looked normal. It looked like home. The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi.
articles.author: Muna Khan

articles.title: Cost of provinces
articles.content: THE cost would be steep. We all knew that. An Islamabad-based think tank has now put figures to those costs. That gives a fiscal dimension to a debate that has largely been driven by political demands and promises of better administration. The Policy Research Institute of Market Economyestimatesthat creating two more provinces in Punjab could add Rs47bn to Rs57bn to annual recurring expenditure. The bill could rise to Rs610bn-Rs730bn if all the country’s 30 divisional units were turned into provinces. Every new province would require a permanent administrative and political structure, including a governor, chief minister, assembly, secretariat and high court. Their salaries, operating expenses and overheads would have to be met year after year, leaving less money for development. The figures expose a major weakness in the argument for creating more provinces: political and administrative restructuring is often presented as an inexpensive way to make government more responsive. It is not. Smaller administrative units create another layer of government whose costs would be hard to justify. If a substantial portion of their allocations goes towards maintaining political and administrative establishments, little would remain for schools, hospitals and other essential services. Citizens promised better governance could end up paying for an expensive new tier without seeing much improvement. There is, of course, a real case for reorganising provincial boundaries. Punjab’s size and population, regional disparities and the sense of political and economic neglect in its southern districts cannot be dismissed. The demand for a separate South Punjab province reflects genuine grievances over unequal development. But these grievances cannot be resolved simply by creating new capitals, assemblies and secretariats. Nor should the fiscal argument be used to brush aside legitimate demands for political representation and administrative autonomy. Can the same objectives be achieved through empowered local governments? Political parties’ record of repeatedly suspending, delaying or weakening elected LGs suggests that the problem is less the size of provinces than the reluctance of political leadership to devolve power and resources. Functional LGs, with predictable funding, elected representatives and clearly defined responsibilities, could take decision-making nearer to citizens without multiplying provincial overheads. Any proposal for provincial restructuring must show how it would improve public services. It must also establish how new units would finance recurring expenditure. The creation of provinces is a long-term fiscal and constitutional commitment. Political parties demanding new provinces must explain how they intend to pay for them and what improvements citizens can expect.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Exchange hack
articles.content: ON Thursday, the largest cryptocurrency heist in history saw some $6.3bn drained from exchange platform Binance’s own wallets. Most of the funds were moved out in about 20 minutes. The hack dwarfed the previous record, of some $1.5bn from rival exchange Bybit in February 2025. Binance’s own investigation initially suggested that the laptop of one of its engineers had been compromised, which allowed attackers to gain access to an internal service used to submit withdrawals. It later emerged that this had been a sophisticated attack involving multiple breach points in Binance’s systems, malicious software that covered its tracks as it operated, and abuse of a feature of the Ethereum network to bypass the exchange’s normal approval controls. Blockchain analytics firms have attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking group. Binance, the largest crypto exchange in the world, has suspended withdrawals as it reviews security. Though Binance has said it will cover all user losses, news of this incident has shaken the crypto sphere. It also raises serious questions — about custody standards, licensing conditions for exchanges, and who bears the losses when things go wrong — for countries in the process of embracing cryptocurrency, including Pakistan. The fact is that Binance is considerably more experienced in the crypto trade than most new entrants and regulators. If its security and operational controls can be compromised, then potentially anyone can be at risk. Until early last year, Pakistan treated crypto as a regulatory no-go area. The authorities have since reversed gear. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao has served as a strategic adviser to the Pakistan Crypto Council since April 2025, and in December 2025 the finance ministry signed an MoU with Binance to explore tokenising up to $2bn in sovereign assets. The exchange’s troubles are therefore of direct concern to Islamabad. But though embracing technology is understandable and perhaps also commendable, policymakers must ensure that the risks that come with dealing in crypto are also being actively assessed and addressed. This incident is a timely reminder that the cost of a security failure can be immense. The authorities need to understand what they are getting into, and make provisions to mitigate risk.
articles.author: Editorial
